tldr: DexFLEX is a low-level foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts from teleoperation or high-level policies into joint commands based on contact stability predicted from tactile feedback, treating drafts as operator intent rather than trajectories to copy. It boosts real-world teleoperation success in tool manipulation from 29.2% to 78.3%, and achieves a 3.5x higher success rate than direct joint-angle prediction when serving as an execution interface for imitation learning.
hero_caption: An overview of DexFLEX. By applying low-level, tactile-based corrections to rough upstream fingertip-motion drafts, it achieves stable dexterous manipulation while maintaining contact. As shown in the bottom-right comparison, while direct execution drops the object given the same draft input, DexFLEX consistently preserves stable contact.
overview:
In dexterous manipulation, such as handling tools or regrasping objects with multi-fingered hands, robots typically receive rough motion commands like "move fingertips here" from human teleoperators or high-level policies. However, these commands lack fine-grained contact details, such as which finger should continue supporting the load or when contacts should switch. As a result, purely following these commands geometrically often leads to failures, such as accidentally releasing a supporting finger and dropping the tool.

To address this, the authors conceived DexFLEX, an approach that reframes upstream motion commands not as trajectories to trace directly, but as online evidence (drafts) for inferring operator intent. From the current proprioceptive and tactile state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion candidates, predicts (Dreams) the contact consequences of each candidate using a latent world model, and selects (Selects) the best candidate that respects intent while avoiding contact failure.

The authors evaluated DexFLEX across simulations with added noise and delays, six long-horizon tool-use tasks on a real-world hand, and as a low-level execution interface for vision-based policy learning.

Remarkably, without any retraining, simply reusing the same trained controller dramatically improved real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3%. Furthermore, in policy learning, it achieved a high success rate that was 3.5x higher than the baseline directly predicting joint angles, demonstrating its effectiveness as a versatile low-level controller.
contributions: Formulated the framework of "command-guided dexterity", which corrects upstream fingertip-motion drafts to maintain tactile-based contact consistency rather than simply following them.
Built DexFLEX, a reusable foundation controller combining state-conditioned motion proposals, latent world model contact prediction, and Draft–Dream–Select inference.

Demonstrated that a single trained model applies across three distinct settings without retraining: degraded-command simulation, real-world shared control for teleoperation, and vision-based policy learning.

sections.heading: From Blindly Copying Commands to Correcting with Intent in Mind
sections.summary: Motion commands from teleoperation or learned policies often omit critical information needed to maintain contact. DexFLEX introduces a reusable foundation controller that treats upstream motion commands as "evidence of intent" and corrects them into motions that preserve contact stability based on tactile feedback.
sections.details:
When operating a multi-fingered hand dexterously, teleoperation gloves or learned upstream policies usually provide rough fingertip-motion drafts over short time windows. Here is the key issue: while this draft shows where the fingertips want to move, it does not specify physical contact decisions—like which finger must keep supporting the load and which should be unloaded. Consequently, even if a motion looks geometrically plausible, the hand might release a supporting finger prematurely or break contact too early, failing the task.

Existing shared autonomy methods and motion prior approaches primarily evaluate consistency with the draft or motion smoothness, without considering what contact consequences the motion will produce. On the other hand, reinforcement learning policies using tactile sensing excel at contact, but they are typically trained end-to-end for specific tasks and do not serve as general-purpose low-level controllers reusable across different upstream modules.

To solve this problem, DexFLEX adopts the principle of "Propose–Predict–Select." It first proposes multiple physically feasible motion candidates conditioned on tactile and proprioceptive states, and predicts their contact consequences with a latent world model. It then selects the candidate that best reflects the original draft's intent while preserving contact, decoding it into joint commands. The breakthrough is that it fixes contact failures while respecting intent, rather than forcefully attenuating or ignoring commands.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Foundation Controllers and Tactile Shared Autonomy
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of two lines of research: motion priors/foundation controllers for dexterous manipulation, and tactile-based shared autonomy. Unlike prior work like DexGen, DexFLEX stands out by selecting motions based not only on motion plausibility but also on predicted contact consequences.
sections.details:
Related prior work falls into two main categories.

The first is "foundation controllers and motion priors for dexterous manipulation." Recently, robot foundation models trained on large-scale datasets to build general-purpose policies have flourished, but most are end-to-end models predicting joint angles directly from camera images. However, multi-fingered hands dealing with delicate contacts require a low-level executor capable of reacting immediately to fine-grained contact changes. Prior works like DexGen proposed foundation controllers generating hand motions from teleoperation commands, but focused heavily on draft matching without predicting whether contact outcomes would be favorable. DexFLEX sets itself apart by decoupling the motion proposal mechanism from the command-based correction mechanism and selecting actions based on predicted contact outcomes.

The second is "shared autonomy and tactile-based contact correction." This approach corrects imperfect human inputs using safety filters or residual policies, but dexterous manipulation introduces contact-specific ambiguity: whether contact is maintained even when commands are satisfied. Traditional tactile policies have typically been trained specifically for single tasks, such as in-hand rotation. DexFLEX treats upstream commands as evidence of intent and reasons over future contacts from tactile states to make selections, elevating the concept of shared autonomy into a general-purpose low-level controller.

sections.heading: How DexFLEX Works: Preventing Contact Failures with Draft–Dream–Select
sections.summary: DexFLEX takes fingertip-motion drafts as input and outputs contact-consistent joint commands. It generates candidates from tactile and proprioceptive states, "Dreams" contact outcomes with a latent world model, scores candidates based on both intent and contact stability, and executes the optimal chunk.
sections.details:
The overall pipeline consists of state encoding, motion candidate proposal, outcome prediction, scoring, and decoding into joint space.

### 3.1 State-Conditioned Motion Proposals
First, the robot's proprioception (e.g., joint angles) and fingertip tactile sensor history are fed into an encoder to produce latent state $s_t=(z_t, g_t)$. The continuous latent variable $z_t=[p_t, c_t]$ consists of proprioceptive token $p_t$ and structured contact token $c_t$. Each finger's taxel array is encoded separately, merged with finger-local proprioceptive features, and aggregated via an attention mechanism. This preserves structure without losing track of which finger supports the load and which is lifted. Additionally, a discrete token $g_t$ representing manipulation phases (like holding, pivoting, or preparing to regrasp) is extracted from a longer time window.

Next, conditioned on this state $s_t$, a Consistency-Flow model generates physically feasible short fingertip motion chunks (trajectories spanning several steps). Operating completely independently of upstream drafts, it defines the plausible motion space itself from the hand's current state.

### 3.2 Outcome-Aware Scoring
To decide which candidate to pick, DexFLEX uses a latent world model $F_\omega$. From the current state $s_t$ and candidate motion $M$, it predicts the latent state at the end of the motion: $\hat{z}_{t+H} = F_\omega(s_t, M)$. This is essentially "dreaming" outcomes in its head.

A learned score function $S_\eta$ then evaluates each candidate by considering the current state, upstream draft $\tilde{M}_t$, candidate motion $M$, and the predicted future contact outcome $F_\omega(s_t, M)$. It is trained to favor motions that maintain supporting contacts even if they slightly deviate from the draft, rather than dangerous motions that simply match the draft closely.

### 3.3 Draft–Dream–Select Execution and Joint Decoding
At inference time, candidates are sampled from two branches. The "Pure-prior branch" samples purely from the prior distribution, serving as a recovery mechanism when the draft is hazardous. The "Draft-seeded branch" initializes from the draft perturbed with moderate noise, ensuring prompt responsiveness to upstream commands. The latent world model predicts outcomes for these combined candidates, and the score function selects the highest-scoring chunk.

The selected fingertip motion is converted into joint commands $a_t$ by an inverse-dynamics decoder. Passing the predicted future contact latent to the decoder allows it to output appropriate joint torques and angles depending on whether the same fingertip displacement should tighten a grasp or release support.

captions.F2: The DexFLEX control pipeline. (1) Proprioceptive and tactile histories are encoded into contact-proprioceptive latent $z_t$ and phase token $g_t$. (2) In Draft–Dream–Select inference, motion candidates are generated from both pure-prior and draft-seeded branches, contact outcomes are predicted via the latent world model, scored, and finally decoded into joint commands.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Inferring Intent and Reliably Preserving Contact
sections.summary: DexFLEX was evaluated in three experiments: recovering degraded commands in simulation, real-world teleoperation across six tool-use tasks, and serving as the execution layer for vision-based imitation learning. Across all settings, it dramatically outperformed baselines in robustness and success rate without any retraining.
sections.details:
The method was evaluated in simulation (Isaac Gym) and on a real robot (16-DoF LEAP hand + 7-DoF xArm7, equipped with FlexiTac tactile sensors).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Baselines included "Raw" (executing upstream drafts directly), "Filter" (low-pass filtering and clipping), "DexGen" (diffusion-based correction using only motion priors), and "DexFLEX w/o Tactile" (DexFLEX stripped of tactile inputs).

### 4.2 Recovering Intent from Degraded Commands
In simulation, four types of degradation were applied to expert commands: noise injection, scaling, delay, and removing commands for supporting fingers. DexFLEX substantially improved task progress and reduced intent recovery error across all degradations. It was particularly effective when supporting-finger commands were removed—a fatal command that usually drops the object. While Raw dropped the object, DexFLEX identified load-bearing fingers via tactile feedback and maintained support contacts while preserving the overall direction of the command. Ablation experiments (Table 1) confirmed that removing outcome evaluation via the score function caused the largest performance drop, proving that simply picking the closest candidate to the draft is insufficient.

### 4.3 Shared Control for Real-World Tool Use
On the real robot, a human operator wearing a data glove performed six tasks: sweeping a brush, turning a nut, hammering, using a screwdriver, serving food with a spatula, and flipping toast (Table 2). Using DexFLEX boosted the average success rate from 29.2% (Raw) to 78.3%, exceeding prior work DexGen (52.5%) by 25.8 percentage points. The difference was especially dramatic in tasks requiring delicate support, such as the spatula and toast-flipping tasks. Furthermore, visualizing intervention intensity in Figure 4 reveals that DexFLEX barely interferes during free transport, intervening strongly only at critical moments when contacts become unstable (scooping or regrasping).

### 4.4 Low-Level Interface for Policy Learning
Vision-based Flow Matching policies were trained with just 50 demonstrations per task, comparing different action output interfaces (Figure 5). Directly predicting joint angles proved extremely fragile with a 13.3% success rate. However, when DexFLEX acted as the executor and the policy predicted only fingertip drafts, success reached 46.7%—a 3.5x improvement over direct joint prediction and 1.56x over DexGen. This demonstrates the strength of decoupling high-level intent learning from low-level contact control.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: DexFLEX is a foundation controller that treats upstream fingertip drafts as intent, elevating them into contact-consistent execution via tactile feedback and outcome prediction. A single trained model works out-of-the-box across diverse settings including teleoperation and policy learning.
sections.details:
DexFLEX is a dexterous manipulation controller operating on the clear philosophy that "upstream commands are not complete trajectories, but evidence of intent," executed through Draft–Dream–Select. In both simulation and real-world experiments, the controller autonomously corrects contacts without requiring human operators or high-level policies to micromanage contact forces, significantly enhancing the reliability of dexterous manipulation.

Best of all, once trained on large-scale simulation data, it offers high versatility—working plug-and-play without any additional training, whether assisting teleoperation or serving as a backend for imitation learning policies. In multi-fingered hand research long plagued by high-dimensional joint spaces and intricate contact dynamics, it holds great promise as a standard interface that cleanly decouples high-level intent from low-level execution.

takeaways: Treating upstream motion commands as "evidence of intent (drafts)" rather than complete trajectories, and separating candidate proposal from selection, is the key to robust dexterous manipulation.
Unlike conventional methods that select motions solely on plausibility, predicting and scoring post-execution contact states using a world model is decisive in preventing contact failures.

Placing a contact-aware controller at the low level relieves high-level visual imitation policies from high-dimensional joint contact dynamics, enabling stable real-world execution with as few as 50 demonstrations.
limitations: In the current implementation, the robot hand embodiment and tactile sensor configuration are fixed, and zero-shot transfer across different hands is not yet addressed.

If the Sim-to-Real gap between tactile simulation and the physical robot is substantial, or if upstream drafts deviate too far from the prior's expected distribution, the controller risks failing to make appropriate corrections.
Because the latent world model's prediction horizon is limited to short intervals, extensions are needed to predict longer-term contact state transitions.
